Assigned
as-si'nd
pp. (appointed; allotted; designated to a person or purpose)
Latin assignare, from ad- and signare, to mark — to mark out for someone. The word carries authority in it: only one with the right to allot can assign.

Biblical Definition

Three occurrences, and they show the word at three moral altitudes. At its best it is mercy institutionalized: “And on the other side Jordan by Jericho eastward, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness upon the plain out of the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead out of the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan out of the tribe of Manasseh” (Josh 20:8). These are cities of refuge, assigned by name and by tribe so that a man who killed without intent had somewhere to run before the avenger of blood reached him. God does not merely command mercy; He gives it a postal address. At its most ordinary it is statecraft: “the priests had a portion assigned them of Pharaoh, and did eat their portion which Pharaoh gave them” (Gen 47:22). And at its worst it is murder written as a duty roster: “And it came to pass, when Joab observed the city, that he assigned Uriah unto a place where he knew that valiant men were” (2Sa 11:16). Nothing in that sentence is illegal. A commander posted a soldier. The whole crime is hidden inside an administrative verb, which is exactly why David thought he could get away with it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines assign as to allot; to appoint or grant by distribution or apportionment; to designate or point out; and in law, to transfer or make over to another.

expand to see more

ASSI'GNED, pp. Appointed; allotted; made over; shown or designated.

ASSI'GN, v.t. [L. assigno, ad and signo, to allot, from signum, a mark.]

1. To allot; to appoint or grant by distribution or apportionment.

The priests had a portion assigned them of Pharaoh. Gen. 47.

2. To designate or point out with precision; as, to assign a reason. 3. In law, to transfer, or make over to another.

Key Scripture

Joshua 20:8 — "And on the other side Jordan by Jericho eastward, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness upon the plain out of the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead out of the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan out of the tribe of Manasseh."

2 Samuel 11:16 — "And it came to pass, when Joab observed the city, that he assigned Uriah unto a place where he knew that valiant men were."

Genesis 47:22 — "Only the land of the priests bought he not; for the priests had a portion assigned them of Pharaoh, and did eat their portion which Pharaoh gave them: wherefore they sold not their lands."

Deuteronomy 19:10 — "That innocent blood be not shed in thy land, which the LORD thy God giveth thee for an inheritance, and so blood be upon thee."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that authority which assigns is accountable for what it assigns men to.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is plain and uncontested. What Scripture attaches to it, however, is a doctrine the age badly needs: that the man who assigns is answerable for the assignment. 2 Samuel 11:16 is the sharpest illustration in the Bible of a crime committed entirely through legitimate channels. Joab did not strike Uriah; he posted him. The order was lawful, the death was plausible, and the paperwork was clean. Nathan's indictment nonetheless goes to David: thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword of the children of Ammon. Distance through a chain of command does not distribute guilt away.

The principle to recover is the one Joshua 20:8 embodies. God assigned the cities of refuge by name, in reachable places, on both sides of Jordan, so that mercy was not left to good intentions. Deuteronomy gives the reason: that innocent blood be not shed in thy land. Authority in Scripture is always granted for the protection of the vulnerable, and any assignment — a posting, a portion, an allotment — is measured by whether it shelters the weak or exposes them. Joab and Joshua used the same verb; they will not receive the same verdict.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hiqdish (H6942), to set apart, sanctify; choq (H2706), a portion decreed; pathan, to give over; Latin assignare, to mark out for.

expand to see more

Hebrew hiqdishu (H6942) — they set apart, consecrated; Joshua 20:8, the cities of refuge sanctified for that use.

Hebrew choq (H2706) — a decreed portion, allowance; Genesis 47:22, the priests' portion from Pharaoh.

Hebrew wayyitten — and he set, placed; 2 Samuel 11:16, Joab placing Uriah at the wall.

Hebrew go'el haddam (H1350, H1818) — the avenger of blood, whom the assigned cities existed to outrun.

Latin assignare, from ad- and signum — to mark out for someone; Webster's root.

Usage

"“They assigned Bezer… and Ramoth… and Golan” — mercy given a postal address."

"“He assigned Uriah unto a place where he knew that valiant men were” — murder as a duty roster."

"“A portion assigned them of Pharaoh” — the ordinary, administrative sense."
